processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots of nominal composition Fe-35Mn-xAl-5Cu (at.%, x = 15, 17, 19) produced by melting high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials in a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere.
Ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h.
Homogenized ingots were hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Plates cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples for Vickers hardness measurements and microstructure characterizations.
Samples were solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching (the parent process proc_st-1100c-10min-oq).
Solution-treated samples were aged at 550 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching. This defines the terminal state of the sample (19Al, 550 °C, 1 h).

structures.overall_structure: Aged 19Al alloy consists of an α (BCC) matrix with a small amount of β-Mn precipitated, the β-Mn forming along α grain boundaries. The α→β-Mn transformation of this highest-Al alloy is thermally activated and slow, so after only 1 h at 550 °C most of the α matrix remains untransformed.
The solution-treated 19Al Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steel is a single-phase α (BCC) structure.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers microhardness measured with an HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester at a load of 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and the average reported.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times, average reported; specimen 10 × 5 × 2 mm³
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure Vickers hardness of the aged alloys to establish the aging hardening behavior
characterization_methods.key_findings: The 19Al alloy aged at 550 °C for 1 h has a Vickers hardness of 524.5 ± 11.6 HV (Table 4).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM operated at 5 kV
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Samples electrolytically polished with a mixture of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify the precipitation of secondary phases such as α-Mn and β-Mn in the aged samples
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 19Al alloy aged at 550 °C for 1 h the SE image (Fig. 9) shows a smooth α matrix with a β-Mn grain-boundary precipitate; β-Mn begins to appear from 550 °C, first decorating α grain boundaries.

unmapped_findings: The increase in Al content slowed down the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn: for the 19Al alloy, the α → β-Mn transformation at 550 °C was only complete after 10 h of aging, versus 6 h for 17Al and much faster for 15Al (b0053, b0065).
The hardness of the 17Al and 19Al alloys increased gradually during low-temperature aging at 525 °C and 550 °C but failed to reach the peak hardness at these temperatures (b0038).
At 550 °C, β-Mn primarily precipitated along α grain boundaries in the 19Al alloy, with a small amount of short rod-shaped β-Mn also observed within α grains (b0053).
The solution-treated 19Al alloy has a Vickers hardness of 263.8 ± 1.1 HV (Table 4), which rises to 524.5 ± 11.6 HV after aging at 550 °C for 1 h.

The 19Al alloy has the highest Al content (18.6 at.% measured by EDS) of the studied series, giving the lowest density (6.66 g·cm⁻³) but the slowest β-Mn precipitation kinetics (Table 1, b0017, b0013).

The overall microstructure evolution sequence during aging of the Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels is reported as: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase (b0068).
